title: F3NO: Frequency-Decomposed Finite-Time Flow-map Neural Operators with Cross-Scale Conditioning

paper.title:
F 3 NO: Frequency-Decomposed Finite-Time Flow-map Neural Operators with
Cross-Scale Conditioning
paper.abstract: Abstract Neural operators enable fast PDE forecasting, but repeated predictions accumulate errors and fine-scale structures remain difficult to resolve. We introduce a frequency-decomposed finite-time flow-map neural operator (F 3 NO) that leverages updated low-frequency features to guide nonlinear refinement of high-frequency information. Within each layer, this cross-scale conditioning connects global spectral processing with local detail refinement. The model directly predicts states at specified future times and adjusts the contributions of the two branches according to the prediction interval. For longer trajectories, it combines parallel predictions within short temporal segments with recursive propagation between segments. Experiments on five PDE benchmarks demonstrate improved forecasting accuracy over autoregressive and direct-prediction baselines. Ablations show that frequency-decomposed refinement can improve accuracy with fewer parameters, while the benefits of segmentation depend on spatial resolution and dynamical regime.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Neural operators (NOs) Lu et al. (2021) ; Kovachki et al. (2023) , particularly Fourier neural operators (FNOs) and their variants Li et al. (2020) ; Tran et al. (2021) ; Guibas et al. (2021) ; Rahman et al. (2022) ; Wen et al. (2022) ; Raonic et al. (2023) ; Liu-Schiaffini et al. (2024) ; Jing et al. (2026) , provide fast surrogate models for learning function-to-function mappings in scientific machine learning Baker et al. (2019) ; Karniadakis et al. (2021) . Their ability to process spatial fields makes them well suited to predicting the evolution of systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Accurate prediction over long horizons, however, remains challenging for nonlinear and chaotic dynamics. A common approach is autoregressive rollout, which repeatedly applies a one-step predictor at a fixed time interval Δ t \Delta_{t} . Errors in predicted states are then propagated through subsequent predictions, potentially causing substantial long-horizon drift. Training through long rollouts can also incur high memory costs and difficult optimization due to the unrolled computation graph Brandstetter et al. (2022) . Several approaches address these temporal prediction challenges. Memory-augmented neural operators incorporate temporal history to improve recurrent predictions Buitrago Ruiz et al. (2025) . Finite-time flow-map learning instead predicts a future state directly from a source state and the elapsed time between them Hirsch et al. (2013) ; Qin et al. (2019) ; Churchill and Xiu (2023) . Time-conditioned neural operators implement this capability by modulating intermediate features according to the requested prediction interval Herde et al. (2024) . Such operators support both direct prediction and recursive composition over shorter intervals. These options provide flexibility in how a trajectory is predicted, but accurate finite-time prediction still requires representing the spatial structures that evolve over each interval. Frequency-dependent prediction errors present a particular challenge. PDE-Refiner demonstrates the importance of non-dominant spatial frequencies and improves their prediction through iterative refinement Lippe et al. (2023) . FreqMoE enhances high-frequency processing by transferring learned low-frequency weights to specialized frequency-domain experts Chen et al. (2025) . These methods motivate treating different parts of the spectrum according to their roles in the prediction problem. Our frequency-resolved analysis further shows that substantial errors can remain in particular spatial frequency bands even when an FNO is conditioned on the prediction interval. Although standard FNO nonlinearities already allow interactions between frequencies, temporal conditioning alone does not specify how an updated global representation should guide the correction of finer-scale features. We therefore investigate an explicit feature pathway that uses the low-frequency update of the current input to condition nonlinear detail refinement. We introduce F 3 NO, a frequency-decomposed finite-time flow-map neural operator built on an FNO backbone. Its central component is a frequency-decomposed spectral refinement (FDSR) block. In each layer, FDSR separates latent features into low- and high-frequency components and updates the low-frequency component through a global Fourier operator. A local nonlinear branch then processes the high-frequency component together with the updated low-frequency features. This conditioning acts on the features of the current input within each layer: the global spectral update directly informs the local detail correction. It differs from transferring weights between frequency experts or iteratively refining an output prediction. A lead-time-dependent fusion mechanism combines the two branches, while feature-wise affine modulation conditions the layer on the prediction interval. By processing high-frequency information through a shared local branch, FDSR also avoids allocating separate spectral weights to those modes. The prediction interval introduces a complementary consideration. Longer intervals reduce the number of recursive transitions but can make the finite-time mapping harder to approximate; shorter intervals simplify each prediction while requiring more frequent propagation of predicted states Luchtenburg et al. (2014) . We use segmented training and execution to examine this trade-off with F 3 NO. The operator is trained to predict over bounded temporal intervals, and long trajectories are generated by propagating predicted states across segment boundaries. Within each segment, intermediate states are predicted directly from the segment’s initial state and can be evaluated in parallel. FDSR thus determines how spatial information is processed, while segmentation determines the temporal interval over which that processing is learned and applied. We evaluate F 3 NO on the 1D Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation (KSE) Kuramoto (1978) ; Ashinsky (1988) , 1D Burgers’ equation (BE) Burgers (1948) , 2D Navier–Stokes equation (NSE) Temam (2001) , 2D shallow-water equation (SWE) Takamoto et al. (2022) , and 3D Rayleigh–Taylor Instability (RTI) Ohana et al. (2024) . Our experiments assess forecasting accuracy, parameter efficiency, and the effects of spatial resolution and prediction interval. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We develop FDSR, an operator-layer architecture in which updated low-frequency features directly condition nonlinear refinement of high-frequency information, with lead-time-dependent fusion of the spectral and local branches. • We investigate segmented training and execution for finite-time neural operators, examining the trade-off between prediction interval and recursive propagation while enabling parallel prediction within each segment. • We evaluate the framework across five PDE benchmarks and use architectural and execution-mode ablations to characterize when frequency refinement and segmentation improve prediction accuracy and efficiency.

sections.heading: 3 Methods: F 3 NO
sections.text: F 3 NO predicts a future PDE state from a source state and a specified time interval. Its central component is frequency-decomposed spectral refinement (FDSR), which uses updated low-frequency features to condition a local nonlinear correction of high-frequency information. We first define the prediction parameterization, then describe the FDSR layers and their segmented training and execution. Figure 1 summarizes the architecture. Figure 1 : Overall architecture. (a) Given a source field u ⁡ ( 𝐱 , t 0 ) u(\mathbf{x},t_{0}) and query time offsets { Δ ​ t i } i = 1 T \{\Delta t_{i}\}_{i=1}^{T} , the model predicts future states u ^ ​ ( 𝐱 , t 0 + Δ ​ t i ) \hat{u}(\mathbf{x},t_{0}+\Delta t_{i}) . (b) Each layer combines a pointwise linear map with FDSR, followed by activation and FiLM conditioning. (c) FDSR separates low- and high-frequency features, uses the updated low-frequency features to condition local detail refinement, and combines the branches through time-dependent gates. (d) FiLM applies channel-wise scale and shift parameters conditioned on the prediction interval.

sections.heading: 3.3 Segmented Training and Prediction
sections.text: Long prediction intervals reduce the number of recursive transitions but can increase the difficulty of approximating each finite-time mapping. Short intervals limit this difficulty while requiring more frequent propagation of predicted states. We use segmented training and prediction to study this trade-off through temporal composition Herde et al. (2024) ; Luchtenburg et al. (2014) . Temporal segmentation. Let τ ≥ 1 \tau\geq 1 denote the number of snapshot intervals per segment, corresponding to a duration τ ​ h 𝒟 \tau h_{\mathcal{D}} . We partition the prediction interval [ 0 , T ] [0,T] into K = ⌈ T / ( τ ​ h 𝒟 ) ⌉ K=\lceil T/(\tau h_{\mathcal{D}})\rceil segments with boundaries 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t K = T , t k + 1 − t k ≤ τ ​ h 𝒟 . 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{K}=T,\qquad t_{k+1}-t_{k}\leq\tau h_{\mathcal{D}}. Training. Our default setting, Hybrid-TF, uses the ground-truth state u t k u_{t_{k}} as the input at each segment boundary. The model directly predicts the observed states within that segment using their respective time displacements. The loss averages snapshot-wise relative L 2 L^{2} errors over the predicted states. This trains the operator on bounded time intervals without propagating prediction errors between training segments. We also consider Hybrid-RO, which feeds the predicted terminal state into the next segment during training. Algorithm 1 in Appendix C details both variants. Prediction. Intermediate choices restrict recursive state propagation to segment boundaries. Their accuracy depends on both the approximation error over each interval and the amplification of boundary errors, which we examine experimentally across segment lengths and dynamical regimes.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We now empirically demonstrate how the proposed components in F 3 NO resolve the issue of prediction error growth across time and frequency scales, leading to general improvements to predictive accuracy across a wide range of PDE systems.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Benchmark. We evaluate F 3 NO on the 1D Burgers’ equation (BE), 1D Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation (KSE), 2D Navier–Stokes equation (NSE), 2D Shallow–Water equation (SWE), and 3D Rayleigh–Taylor Instability (RTI). These datasets cover nonlinear convection, dissipative dynamics, and chaotic time evolution. Data generation and prediction settings are detailed in Appendix A . Baselines. As baselines of comparison, we consider methods from two broad classes: rollout and flow-map. Rollout-based methods are trained either in pure rollout mode or using teacher forcing (TF). We evaluate FNO Li et al. (2020) , FFNO Tran et al. (2021) , UNet Gupta and Brandstetter (2022) , S4FFNO Buitrago Ruiz et al. (2025) , PDE-Refiner Lippe et al. (2023) , and FreqMoE Chen et al. (2025) . Flow-map-based baselines directly learn a finite-time solution operator that maps between states separated by arbitrary time gaps, including a simple MLP, DeepONets (DONs) Lu et al. (2021) , TCIN Herde et al. (2024) , and HyperFNO Alesiani et al. (2022) . Training and testing. Given a discrete-time trajectory { u t } t = 0 T \{u_{t}\}_{t=0}^{T} , the goal of neural operator training is to predict the full trajectory from the initial state u 0 u_{0} . For all methods, the models make predictions on a trajectory { u ^ t } t = 1 T \{\hat{u}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} . For training, we compute a mean solution-snapshot-wise normalized error. For testing, we provide a novel initial condition to the trained model and collect a predicted trajectory, u ^ 1 : T \hat{u}_{1:T} . Then we evaluate the model performance using the normalized root mean square error (nRMSE), nRMSE = 1 n test ∑ k = 1 n test ‖ u 1 : T ( k ) − u ^ 1 : T ( k ) ‖ 2 / ‖ u 1 : T ( k ) ‖ 2 \mathrm{nRMSE}=\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{k=1}^{n_{\text{test}}}{\left\|u_{1:T}^{(k)}-\hat{u}_{1:T}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}}/{\left\|u_{1:T}^{(k)}\right\|_{2}} , where u 1 : T {u}_{1:T} refers to the ground-truth trajectory, the superscript (k) indicates the k k -th trajectory, and n test n_{\text{test}} refers to the number of test trajectories. Unless otherwise stated, F 3 NO denotes the FNO backbone equipped with FDSR and FiLM conditioning, trained with Hybrid-TF and evaluated using segmented flow-map execution. The segment length is fixed to τ = 4 \tau=4 for KSE, NSE, and RTI, τ = 10 \tau=10 for SWE, and τ = 19 \tau=19 for BE. The low-frequency spectral branch uses approximately three-quarters of the available Fourier modes on BE and KSE, 16 modes on NSE and SWE, and 12 modes on RTI.

This indicates that explicitly separating and coupling different frequency components improves the quality of the finite-time predictor. Although FDSR improves prediction accuracy, FNO-Flow-map+FDSR still exhibits substantial errors at longer lead times in this example. This motivates limiting the temporal span of each prediction through segmented training and execution. sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Neural operators provide a framework for learning mappings between functions across discretizations. The FNO Li et al. (2020) parameterizes integral kernels in the frequency domain. Subsequent work improves efficiency and expressivity: Factorized FNO (FFNO) Tran et al. (2021) uses separable spectral layers, S4FFNO Buitrago Ruiz et al. (2025) incorporates temporal memory through state-space modeling, and AFNO Guibas et al. (2021) introduces efficient Fourier-domain channel mixing and soft-thresholding. U-NO Rahman et al. (2022) , U-FNO Wen et al. (2022) , and U-Net variants Gupta and Brandstetter (2022) use hierarchical or complementary local processing to capture multiscale structure. HyperFNO Alesiani et al. (2022) instead uses hypernetworks to generate operator weights conditioned on PDE parameters. Spectral bias Rahaman et al. (2019) and Fourier-mode truncation can hinder fine-scale prediction, motivating frequency-aware designs. PDE-Refiner Lippe et al. (2023) iteratively refines predicted states to recover non-dominant frequency information. Spectral-Refiner Cao et al. (2025) fine-tunes an untruncated spatiotemporal spectral layer using a PDE-residual-based objective, while FreqMoE Chen et al. (2025) transfers learned low-frequency weights to high-frequency experts. Our FDSR block instead decomposes latent features and uses the updated low-frequency representation of the current input to condition nonlinear refinement of the high-frequency branch within each operator layer. This distinguishes its feature-level conditioning from output-state refinement, spectral-layer fine-tuning, and weight transfer. For time-dependent systems, neural operators are often deployed autoregressively, repeatedly mapping u t u_{t} to u t + Δ t u_{t+\Delta_{t}} at a fixed time step. This sequential dependence can accumulate prediction errors and increase long-horizon inference latency. Neural ODEs Chen et al. (2018) represent continuous-time dynamics through learned derivatives but require numerical integration. Neural flows Biloš et al. (2021) ; Boffi et al. (2025b) and time-conditioned operators Herde et al. (2024) directly parameterize finite-time mappings. Building on this formulation, we combine FDSR with segmented execution to balance finite-time mapping difficulty against recursive error propagation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced F 3 NO, a frequency-decomposed finite-time flow-map neural operator for accurate and efficient PDE forecasting. The Frequency-Decomposed Spectral Refinement uses updated low-frequency features to guide nonlinear high-frequency refinement, explicitly connecting global spectral processing with local detail correction. This improves the representation of fine-scale dynamics while providing a parameter-efficient mechanism for processing high-frequency information. Lead-time-dependent fusion further adjusts the contributions of the low- and high-frequency branches to the prediction interval. Complementing this architecture, segmented training and prediction balance the difficulty of learning long-range mappings against recursive error accumulation. By predicting states directly within each segment and propagating predictions only across segment boundaries, the framework reduces sequential dependence and can improve long-horizon accuracy. Across five PDE benchmarks, F 3 NO achieves the lowest mean prediction error across all evaluated settings. These results demonstrate the value of combining explicit cross-scale conditioning with flexible temporal composition for long-horizon prediction of complex PDE dynamics.

sections.heading: 1D Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Equation.
sections.text:
The Kuramoto–Sivashinsky Equation (KSE) is a nonlinear, dissipative partial differential equation that exhibits spatiotemporal chaos, making it a widely adopted testbed for studying long-term prediction, stability, and error accumulation in learned dynamical models. Its well-understood physical structure and extensive use in prior work allow for direct and meaningful comparison with existing NO approaches. sections.heading: B.1 Rollout Baselines
sections.text: Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [ 30 ] : FNO learns a resolution-invariant mapping between function spaces by (i) lifting the input field to a latent channel space, (ii) applying a stack of Fourier operator blocks that combine a non-local spectral operator with local pointwise maps and nonlinearities, and (iii) projecting back to the solution space. A single FNO block can be written as v ( ℓ + 1 ) ​ ( x ) = σ ⁡ ( W ( ℓ ) ​ v ( ℓ ) ​ ( x ) + 𝒦 ( ℓ ) ​ ( ϕ ) ​ v ( ℓ ) ​ ( x ) ) , v^{(\ell+1)}(x)=\sigma\Big(W^{(\ell)}v^{(\ell)}(x)+\mathcal{K}^{(\ell)}(\phi)v^{(\ell)}(x)\Big), (19) where 𝒦 ( ℓ ) \mathcal{K}^{(\ell)} denotes the learned kernel integral operator parameterized by ϕ \phi , W ( ℓ ) W^{(\ell)} is a local linear map, and σ \sigma is a pointwise nonlinearity. Factorized Fourier Neural Operators (FFNOs) [ 51 ] : To address computational bottlenecks in high-dimensional settings and enable the training of deeper architectures, the factorized Fourier neural operator (FFNO) [ 51 ] introduces a separable spectral layer. Instead of a full d d -dimensional Fourier transform, FFNO factorizes the operation across each spatial dimension independently. The kernel operator is decomposed into a sum of spectral convolutions over dimensions j ∈ { 1 , … , d } j\in\{1,\dots,d\} : 𝒦 fac ( ℓ ) ​ ( ϕ ) ​ v ( ℓ ) ​ ( x ) = ∑ j = 1 d ℱ j − 1 ​ ( R ϕ , j ⋅ ℱ j ​ ( v ( ℓ ) ) ) ​ ( x ) , \mathcal{K}^{(\ell)}_{\text{fac}}(\phi)v^{(\ell)}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\mathcal{F}_{j}^{-1}\Big(R_{\phi,j}\cdot\mathcal{F}_{j}(v^{(\ell)})\Big)(x), (20) where ℱ j \mathcal{F}_{j} is the 1D Fourier transform along dimension j j . Furthermore, FFNO adopts an enhanced residual block structure to improve gradient flow. The update rule for layer l l incorporates a two-layer feedforward network (MLP) mixed with the spectral convolution: v ( ℓ + 1 ) ​ ( x ) = v ( ℓ ) ​ ( x ) + σ ⁡ ( W 2 ( ℓ ) ​ σ ​ ( W 1 ( ℓ ) ​ ( 𝒦 fac ( ℓ ) ​ ( ϕ ) ​ v ( ℓ ) ​ ( x ) ) + b 1 ( ℓ ) ) + b 2 ( ℓ ) ) , v^{(\ell+1)}(x)=v^{(\ell)}(x)+\sigma\left(W_{2}^{(\ell)}\sigma\left(W_{1}^{(\ell)}(\mathcal{K}^{(\ell)}_{\text{fac}}(\phi)v^{(\ell)}(x))+b_{1}^{(\ell)}\right)+b_{2}^{(\ell)}\right), (21) where { W i } \{W_{i}\} are local linear transformations and { b i } \{b_{i}\} are biases. This format significantly reduces the parameter count and computational complexity while maintaining the global receptive field. U-Net Neural Operator (U-Net) [ 20 ] : As a convolutional encoder-decoder baseline, we use a U-Net style with skip connections. It consists of four downsampling convolution blocks, a middle bottleneck block, and four upsampling convolution blocks. The upsampling path uses the standard U-Net design with skip connections between corresponding stages in the encoder and decoder. We use channel multipliers [1,2,2,2], do not employ explicit time embeddings, and set the first dimension to 32. S4 Factorized Fourier Neural Operator (S4FFNO) [ 11 ] : S4FFNO is a memory-augmented model that instantiates the MemNO framework by combining FFNO as a Markovian neural operator with an explicit sequential memory layer based on S4 [ 18 ] . Concretely, the spatial operator layers are applied timestep-wise as in FFNO, while memory is introduced by inserting a causal sequence model M M on a chosen hidden layer to aggregate information from past states. In S4FFNO, this memory module is implemented with an S4 layer operating independently at each spatial location x x , i.e., v ~ ( k ) ​ ( t i , x ) = S4 ⁡ ( v ( k ) ​ ( t i , x ) , v ( k ) ​ ( t i − 1 , x ) , … , v ( k ) ​ ( t 0 , x ) ) , \tilde{v}^{(k)}(t_{i},x)\;=\;\mathrm{S4}\Big(v^{(k)}(t_{i},x),\,v^{(k)}(t_{i-1},x),\,\ldots,\,v^{(k)}(t_{0},x)\Big), (22) and the resulting v ~ ( k ) ​ ( t i , ⋅ ) \tilde{v}^{(k)}(t_{i},\cdot) is then passed through the remaining FFNO layers. The main motivation is that standard one-step objectives tend to emphasize dominant, high-amplitude frequency components, while low-amplitude components may be underrepresented and accumulate into substantial errors during long rollouts. Following the diffusion-based formulation of PDE-Refiner, we predict the temporal residual rather than the next state directly. Given the current state u t u_{t} , we define the normalized residual as r t + 1 = u t + 1 − u t c out , r_{t+1}=\frac{u_{t+1}-u_{t}}{c_{\mathrm{out}}}, (23) where c out c_{\mathrm{out}} is a dataset-dependent output factor used to normalize the residual scale. Specifically, for KSE with ν ∈ { 0.075 , 0.1 , 0.125 } \nu\in\{0.075,0.1,0.125\} , we use c out ∈ { 0.4 , 0.18 , 0.12 } c_{\mathrm{out}}\in\{0.4,0.18,0.12\} , respectively. We set c out = 0.008 c_{\mathrm{out}}=0.008 for SWE, c out = 0.12 c_{\mathrm{out}}=0.12 for BE, and c out = 0.0125 c_{\mathrm{out}}=0.0125 for RTI. These factors are computed from the corresponding temporal residuals at resolution S = 128 S=128 for KSE and BE, 64 × 64 64\times 64 for NSE and SWE, and 32 × 32 × 32 32\times 32\times 32 for RTI. FreqMoE [ 15 ] : FreqMoE augments Fourier Neural Operators with frequency-domain mixture-of-experts to improve the modeling of high-frequency components. It follows a low-frequency pretraining and high-frequency fine-tuning (LPHF) paradigm. A low-frequency FNO is first pretrained and then upcycled into a frequency-domain mixture-of-experts model, where the pretrained spectral weights are retained as the low-frequency base component and specialized high-frequency experts are introduced through low-rank adaptation. The frequency spectrum beyond the base band is partitioned into disjoint regions assigned to different experts, while a learnable gating mechanism controls their contributions. For FreqMoE, we adopt the same FNO backbone and dataset-specific configurations as our FNO baselines. Following the LPHF paradigm, the low-frequency FNO is pretrained for 100 epochs and then sparsely upcycled from its final checkpoint for 100 epochs of high-frequency fine-tuning, preserving the same total 200-epoch training budget as baselines. For BE and KSE at spatial resolution S = 128 S=128 , the pretrained FNO uses 48 Fourier modes and the high-frequency experts extend the spectral support to all 65 nonnegative Fourier modes. For NSE and SWE at resolution 64 × 64 64\times 64 , the pretrained FNO uses 16 modes per spatial dimension and sparse upcycling extends the spectral support to ( 32 , 33 ) (32,33) , corresponding to the full real-valued Fourier spectrum. For RTI at resolution 32 × 32 × 32 32\times 32\times 32 , the pretrained FNO uses 12 modes per spatial dimension and sparse upcycling extends the spectral support to ( 16 , 16 , 17 ) (16,16,17) , corresponding to the full real-valued Fourier spectrum. We use LoRA [ 24 ] rank 4, a sparsity regularization weight of 0.01, and Top-1, Top-2, and Top-5 expert activation for the 1D, 2D, and 3D benchmarks, respectively. Both the pretraining and fine-tuning stages use one-step teacher forcing, while evaluation is performed through fully autoregressive rollout.

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
sections.text: In this section, we provide a detailed description of our training strategies for autoregressive rollouts, model specifications, and the hardware configurations used in our experiments.

sections.heading: C.1 Training Strategies for Autoregressive Rollouts
sections.text: Let { u t } t = 0 T t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l \{u^{t}\}_{t=0}^{T_{total}} denote a discrete-time trajectory and let ℳ \mathcal{M} denote a one-step predictor. Rollout (autoregressive) : In rollout setting, the model is trained and evaluated by feeding back its own predicted states as inputs for subsequent steps: u ^ t + 1 = ℳ ⁡ ( u ^ t ) , u ^ 0 = u 0 . \hat{u}^{t+1}=\mathcal{M}(\hat{u}^{t}),\qquad\hat{u}^{0}=u^{0}. (29) Markov teacher forcing (TF) : In teacher forcing, the model is trained with the ground-truth previous state as input, while the model is evaluated autoregressively: u ^ t + 1 = ℳ ⁡ ( u t ) (train) , u ^ t + 1 = ℳ ⁡ ( u ^ t ) (test) . \hat{u}^{t+1}=\mathcal{M}(u^{t})\quad\text{(train)},\qquad\hat{u}^{t+1}=\mathcal{M}(\hat{u}^{t})\quad\text{(test)}. (30) We use a first-order (Markov) conditioning scheme, i.e., the model conditions only on the immediately preceding state.

sections.heading: Two training modes.
sections.text: The segmented flow-map framework introduced in Section 3.3 admits two operational modes during training. In Segmented Rollout (Hybrid-RO), the predicted terminal state of each segment is recursively fed into the next segment, enabling fully autonomous inference. In Segmented Teacher Forcing (Hybrid-TF), the model is re-grounded using ground-truth states at segment boundaries during training, which stabilizes optimization by preventing early prediction errors from corrupting subsequent segments. The distinction is made explicit in Algorithm 1 .

sections.heading: Limiting cases and trade-offs.
sections.text: The segment length τ \tau interpolates between two extremes: τ = 1 ⇒ standard autoregressive rollout , τ = T ⇒ single global flow-map . \begin{split}\tau&=1\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;\text{standard autoregressive rollout},\\ \tau&=T\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;\text{single global flow-map}.\end{split} (31) Intermediate values of τ \tau define a continuum of execution regimes that balance local stability and global efficiency. Smaller segments reduce the difficulty of learning long-range mappings at the cost of more frequent recursion, while larger segments improve computational efficiency but increase the burden on the flow-map operator. By explicitly bridging rollouts and flow-map at the operational level, segmented execution provides a flexible mechanism for stabilizing long-horizon prediction without sacrificing the core advantages of the flow-map prediction formulation. sections.heading: C.3 Training Details
sections.text: All methods are implemented in Python using PyTorch [ 42 ] , building on the original implementation of FNOs [ 30 ] , and following the experimental setup in [ 11 ] . All models are trained for 200 epochs using the AdamW optimizer [ 35 ] with an initial learning rate of 0.001, weight decay 0.0001, and a cosine-annealing learning-rate schedule. The batch sizes are set to 32 for KSE, 64 for BE, 20 for NSE, 10 for SWE, and 1 for RTI. For each configuration, we run three independent experiments with varying random seeds and report results averaged over three runs of the test loss at the final training epoch. Experiments are conducted on Nvidia RTX 4090 and A100 GPUs in a single-GPU setup. Although we do not optimize our code particularly to minimize the inference time, the proposed FiLM-only baselines naturally take less time per epoch to train compared to rollout-based methods. For our standard NSE setup, baselines with only FiLM module take around 40 seconds per epoch, while the rollout-based methods take roughly 120 seconds per epoch.

sections.heading: C.4 Model Specification
sections.text: For all FNO backbones, we use a unified architecture and hyper-parameter configuration to control for model capacity. Specifically, we employ four Fourier layers. For KSE and BE, all non-frequency-decomposed models use the full set of spectral modes, i.e., k m ​ a ​ x = ⌊ S / 2 ⌋ k_{max}=\lfloor S/2\rfloor (where S S is the spatial resolution). For NSE, we follow the setting used in prior baselines [ 51 , 11 ] to use 16 Fourier modes. For SWE, we use 16 Fourier modes. For RTI, we use 12 Fourier modes. We set the width to d v = 128 d_{v}=128 for KSE and BE, while for NSE, SWE, and RTI, we use d v = 64 d_{v}=64 . The input is lifted to d v d_{v} channels by a linear layer, and the output is projected back to solution space using a two-layer MLP with one hidden layer, the hidden dimension is 256 for KSE and BE, 128 for NSE, SWE, and RTI. The expanded hidden dimension of the feedforward MLP of FFNO is 4 ⋅ d v 4\cdot d_{v} . The nonlinearity functions are GELU [ 21 ] for KSE and BE, and RELU [ 40 ] for NSE, SWE, and RTI. For our proposed time-conditioned variants, we use a single-layer MLP with width d v d_{v} to generate the FiLM modulation parameters γ ⁡ ( Δ t ) \gamma(\Delta_{t}) and β ⁡ ( Δ t ) \beta(\Delta_{t}) , where Δ t \Delta_{t} is normalized by the total prediction horizon or by the segment length seg in the segmented execution setting. This FiLM hypernetwork is trained with a learning rate that is 10 × 10\times larger than the backbone learning rate, while all other optimizer settings remain unchanged.

sections.heading: D.2 Cross-Scale Conditioning and Local-Refinement
sections.text: We examine two architectural choices in FDSR through ablations on KSE (Table 4 ) and NSE (Table 5 ). First, we assess whether information from lower frequencies helps refine features at higher frequencies. We compare three versions of the refinement branch. The first version (“High-freq only") receives only the features at higher frequencies, while the second (“High-freq concat with original low-freq") also receives the original features at lower frequencies. In F 3 NO, the spectral operator first updates the features at lower frequencies before passing them to the refinement branch alongside the features at higher frequencies. Second, we test whether adding local nonlinear processing can provide the same benefit without separating the features by frequency. We replace the refinement branch with a pointwise MLP (“MLP local branch") that receives the full, undecomposed latent features. The resulting model has a comparable number of parameters. All four refinement variants retain the spectral branch for the lower frequencies and use the same time conditioning. Each uses Hybrid-TF with τ = 4 \tau=4 . Across both benchmarks, the full FDSR block achieves the lowest mean error at every tested viscosity. Providing the original features at lower frequencies improves upon refinement using only the features at higher frequencies. Updating those features through the spectral operator further reduces the mean error in every setting. These results support updating the information at lower frequencies before using it to guide refinement at higher frequencies. The MLP control also yields higher mean errors at comparable parameter counts, suggesting that additional nonlinear capacity alone does not explain the improvement.

sections.heading: Frequency-decomposed spectral refinement used in autoregressive rollout.
sections.text: The first two row blocks, Rollout and Rollout with Frequency-Decomposed Spectral Refinement (FDSR), compare standard FNO/FFNO models trained with teacher forcing (TF) against their FDSR-equipped counterparts, also trained with TF. When using FDSR with 40 or 48 retained modes, where the retained modes model the low-frequency component and the remaining modes are used for high-frequency refinement, the proposed method consistently improves prediction accuracy over the standard counterparts. These results suggest that inter-frequency mixing through frequency-decomposed refinement provides clear benefits even in the standard rollout setting.

sections.heading: Ablation on the architectural choices: FiLM only or FDSR + FiLM.
sections.text: To test the effectiveness of the FDSR, we compare the performance of the models with FiLM only and with FDSR + FiLM. Regardless of the choice of the backbone network and also regardless of the operation modes (i.e., flow-map or hybrid), adding FDSR provides improvement in terms of prediction accuracy as well as decreased model parameter counts. This result suggests that the FDSR not only serves as an effective tool for mixing inter-frequency information, but also as an efficient alternative for modeling high-frequency modes.

sections.heading: Ablation on the operation modes: Rollout or Flow-map or Hybrid.
sections.text: The results clearly show that relying on a single operation mode (either Rollout or Flow-map) does not provide the best performance results. Regardless of the time-conditioning mechanisms (FiLM or FDSR+FiLM), the hybrid method (i.e., the segmented rollout) produces prediction results that outperform both baselines (rollout and flow-map). Tables 7 – 8 report the same comparison at lower spatial resolutions, S = 64 S=64 and S = 32 S=32 . A different pattern emerges from the high-resolution setting. FDSR continues to improve the direct flow-map predictor at both resolutions. For example, at S = 64 S=64 , adding FDSR reduces the FiLM-only flow-map error from 4.11 % 4.11\% to 2.95 % 2.95\% at ν = 0.075 \nu=0.075 , and at S = 32 S=32 from 5.62 % 5.62\% to 3.91 % 3.91\% . Similar improvements are observed for the other viscosities. This indicates that the frequency-decomposed refinement remains useful even when the spatial representation is coarser. In contrast, segmented execution provides little additional benefit at these lower resolutions. The direct FNO-Flow-map+FDSR and F 3 NO results are nearly identical at both S = 64 S=64 and S = 32 S=32 . This suggests that, after spatial coarsening removes much of the fine-scale complexity, a single finite-time flow-map can already model the full prediction horizon effectively. In these settings, further segmentation is unnecessary because the long-range mapping is sufficiently tractable. The benefit of Hybrid-TF therefore becomes more pronounced as spatial resolution increases, whereas at lower resolutions direct full-horizon prediction can be sufficient. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly modeling the distinct behaviors of low- and high-frequency components provides a useful inductive bias for time-conditioned prediction. For the FDSR variants, we set the spectral cutoff to approximately three quarters of the full modes: specifically, m = 48 m=48 for S = 128 S=128 , m = 24 m=24 for S = 64 S=64 , and m = 12 m=12 for S = 32 S=32 . Empirically, this choice provides a favorable accuracy–parameter trade-off while preserving a nontrivial set of high-frequency components for the refinement branch.

sections.heading: Appendix E Segmented Training and Prediction
sections.text: We examine how segmentation affects prediction accuracy across time-conditioned operators, spatial resolutions, and dynamical regimes. The segment length τ \tau specifies the number of snapshot intervals per segment, with τ = 1 \tau=1 corresponding to one-step autoregression and a segment spanning the full horizon corresponding to direct prediction. Shorter segments limit the interval covered by each prediction but require more recursive transitions, while longer segments reduce these transitions at the cost of potentially harder finite-time mappings. We first compare time-conditioned operators under direct and segmented prediction, then examine the effects of segment length and training strategy across PDE benchmarks. Hybrid-TF uses ground-truth segment-boundary states during training, whereas Hybrid-RO propagates predicted states between training segments. Both use predicted boundary states at inference. Finally, we evaluate a complementary error-propagation diagnostic that assesses candidate execution intervals using a fixed trained model and compare its preferred interval with the empirical sweep results.

sections.heading: E.1 Effect of Segmentation across Time-Conditioned Operators

TCIN [ 22 ] combined with FNO and FFNO (denoted as FNO-TCIN and FFNO-TCIN, respectively) provides the closest architectural baseline to our proposed method, as TCIN also employs hypernetwork-based FiLM-style shift-and-scale modulation for time-displacement conditioning. We further evaluate the proposed segmented execution strategy on BE, KSE, NSE, SWE, and RTI benchmarks, as shown in Figures 7 – 10 . All considered methods are variants of F 3 NOs and the naming convention is FNO-Hybrid-[operation-mode], where the operation-mode ∈ \in {RO, TF}. In all five benchmarks, the case τ = 1 	au=1 corresponds to the pure autoregressive rollout, while the largest segment length in each plot, i.e., τ = 19 	au=19 for BE, τ = 24 	au=24 for KSE and RTI, τ = 19 , 29 , 49 	au=19,29,49 for the three NSE viscosity ( 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3} ), and τ = 100 	au=100 for SWE, corresponds to the single global finite-time flow-map prediction over the full available horizon. These results highlight how the optimal segment length depends on both the underlying dynamics and the prediction horizon. Across the BE and KSE benchmarks, the pure rollout generally produces the largest prediction errors, confirming that stepwise autoregression is vulnerable to long-horizon error accumulation. For these 1D systems, increasing the segment length often improves performance, and the global flow-map can be competitive, especially at lower spatial resolutions and at higher viscosity, where the dynamics are smoother and the long-range mapping is easier to approximate. In the NSE benchmark with chosen specific viscosity values ( 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3} ), the resulting dynamics appear to be more complex and both extremes (i.e., pure rollout and pure flow-map) become less optimal: τ = 1 	au=1 suffers from recursive error accumulation, while the full-horizon segment also yields large errors because the model must directly learn a highly nonlinear mapping between temporally distant and weakly correlated states. Intermediate segment lengths therefore achieve better performance by balancing these two sources of error. Similar results are observed in the SWE and RTI benchmarks. Segmented Autoregressive Rollout or Segmented Teacher Forcing : The results also compare two segmented execution strategies: Hybrid-RO and Hybrid-TF. Hybrid-RO trains the model under a segmented rollout setting, where predicted segment-boundary states are recursively used to initialize subsequent segments. This setting better matches long-horizon inference, but it is more sensitive to boundary prediction errors. Hybrid-TF, in contrast, re-grounds the model with ground-truth segment-boundary states during training, which can stabilize optimization by preventing early errors from contaminating later segments. The comparisons between Hybrid-RO and Hybrid-TF further show that the preferred training strategy depends on the complexity of the target dynamics. Hybrid-RO is mainly competitive in relatively easier settings, such as BE and the low-resolution KSE case, where predicted segment-boundary states can be propagated with small drift. In more challenging settings, including higher resolution KSE and the two-dimensional NSE benchmark, Hybrid-TF often yields lower or more stable errors by re-grounding segment boundaries during training, which helps prevent early segment-boundary errors from accumulating across subsequent segments. SWE and RTI benchmarks show a similar trend to the NSE benchmark, with Hybrid-TF being the robust choice in the more challenging long-horizon settings. Overall, these results support the motivation for segmented hybrid execution. Rather than committing to either pure rollouts or a single global flow-map, the proposed strategy provides a trade-off between the two. This allows the model to reduce stepwise error accumulation while avoiding the optimization difficulty of overly long one-shot finite-time prediction.

sections.heading: E.4 Irregularly Sampled Measurements
sections.text: We further evaluate robustness under irregular temporal sampling, a common setting in which measurements are missing due to non-uniform acquisition. While rollouts can still be applied by advancing between observed states, their reliance on stepwise continuity makes them increasingly sensitive to missing data. In contrast, flow-map-based models naturally map between states separated by arbitrary time gaps, making them better suited for irregularly sampled trajectories. This experiment assesses whether the proposed segmented flow-map retains this advantage under substantial temporal sparsity. Starting from fully sampled KSE trajectories, we randomly remove a fixed fraction of time steps from each trajectory, with missing percentages 20%, 40%, 60% and 80%. The remaining observations are used as inputs, and models are tasked with predicting the system evolution across the resulting non-uniform temporal gaps. Figure 11 : [KSE, ν = 0.075 \nu=0.075 , S = 64 S=64 ] Relative L 2 L^{2} error versus missing time-step percentage under irregular temporal sampling. Missing masks are sampled independently per test trajectory, with t = 0 t=0 and the final prediction time retained. Ours refers to our main FNO-Hybrid-TF model. Figure 11 reports the test error as a function of the missing percentage. As the fraction of missing data increases, all methods exhibit performance degradation; however, rollout-based approaches degrade rapidly due to accumulated error across increasingly long effective time steps. Direct flow-map baselines show improved robustness but still struggle when the temporal gaps become large. In contrast, the proposed segmented flow-map consistently achieves the lowest error across all missing rates and degrades most gracefully as sparsity increases. This behavior highlights a key strength of the proposed approach: by combining finite-time flow-map prediction with controlled segmentation, the method can reliably bridge irregular temporal gaps while avoiding the instability inherent to dense rollouts.

sections.heading: Appendix F Limitations
sections.text: Despite the promising empirical performance, the proposed framework has several limitations that warrant further investigation. First, the segmentation length τ \tau in the hybrid execution strategy is currently treated as a user-defined hyperparameter, and its optimal value can vary depending on the underlying dynamics and spatial resolution. Second, the frequency decomposition relies on a fixed spectral cutoff, whereas adaptive frequency partitioning may provide additional flexibility across different PDE regimes. Finally, although the proposed framework exhibits stable and accurate long-horizon prediction empirically, further theoretical understanding of its stability and error propagation properties would be valuable.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.10998v1 [cs.LG] 07 Oct 2026 F 3 NO: Frequency-Decomposed Finite-Time Flow-map Neural Operators with Cross-Scale Conditioning Fan Wu Affiliation: Arizona State University Affiliation: Tempe, AZ Email: fanwu8@asu.edu Cheng Jing Affiliation: Arizona State University Affiliation: Tempe, AZ Email: cjing6@asu.edu Kookjin Lee Affiliation: Arizona State University Affiliation: Tempe, AZ Email: klee263@asu.edu Abstract Neural operators enable fast PDE forecasting, but repeated predictions accumulate errors and fine-scale structures remain difficult to resolve. We introduce a frequency-decomposed finite-time flow-map neural operator (F 3 NO) that leverages updated low-frequency features to guide nonlinear refinement of high-frequency information. Within each layer, this cross-scale conditioning connects global spectral processing with local detail refinement. The model directly predicts states at specified future times and adjusts the contributions of the two branches according to the prediction interval. For longer trajectories, it combines parallel predictions within short temporal segments with recursive propagation between segments. Experiments on five PDE benchmarks demonstrate improved forecasting accuracy over autoregressive and direct-prediction baselines. Ablations show that frequency-decomposed refinement can improve accuracy with fewer parameters, while the benefits of segmentation depend on spatial resolution and dynamical regime. 1 Introduction Neural operators (NOs) Lu et al. (2021) ; Kovachki et al. (2023) , particularly Fourier neural operators (FNOs) and their variants Li et al. (2020) ; Tran et al. (2021) ; Guibas et al. (2021) ; Rahman et al. (2022) ; Wen et al. (2022) ; Raonic et al. (2023) ; Liu-Schiaffini et al. (2024) ; Jing et al. (2026) , provide fast surrogate models for learning function-to-function mappings in scientific machine learning Baker et al. (2019) ; Karniadakis et al. (2021) . Their ability to process spatial fields makes them well suited to predicting the evolution of systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs). Accurate prediction over long horizons, however, remains challenging for nonlinear and chaotic dynamics. A common approach is autoregressive rollout, which repeatedly applies a one-step predictor at a fixed time interval Δ t \Delta_{t} . Errors in predicted states are then propagated through subsequent predictions, potentially causing substantial long-horizon drift. Training through long rollouts can also incur high memory costs and difficult optimization due to the unrolled computation graph Brandstetter et al. (2022) . Several approaches address these temporal prediction challenges. Memory-augmented neural operators incorporate temporal history to improve recurrent predictions Buitrago Ruiz et al. (2025) . Finite-time flow-map learning instead predicts a future state directly from a source state and the elapsed time between them Hirsch et al. (2013) ; Qin et al. (2019) ; Churchill and Xiu (2023) . Time-conditioned neural operators implement this capability by modulating intermediate features according to the requested prediction interval Herde et al. (2024) . Such operators support both direct prediction and recursive composition over shorter intervals. These options provide flexibility in how a trajectory is predicted, but accurate finite-time prediction still requires representing the spatial structures that evolve over each interval. Frequency-dependent prediction errors present a particular challenge. PDE-Refiner demonstrates the importance of non-dominant spatial frequencies and improves their prediction through iterative refinement Lippe et al. (2023) . FreqMoE enhances high-frequency processing by transferring learned low-frequency weights to specialized frequency-domain experts Chen et al. (2025) . These methods motivate treating different parts of the spectrum according to their roles in the prediction problem. Our frequency-resolved analysis further shows that substantial errors can remain in particular spatial frequency bands even when an FNO is conditioned on the prediction interval. Although standard FNO nonlinearities already allow interactions between frequencies, temporal conditioning alone does not specify how an updated global representation should guide the correction of finer-scale features. We therefore investigate an explicit feature pathway that uses the low-frequency update of the current input to condition nonlinear detail refinement. We introduce F 3 NO, a frequency-decomposed finite-time flow-map neural operator built on an FNO backbone. Its central component is a frequency-decomposed spectral refinement (FDSR) block. In each layer, FDSR separates latent features into low- and high-frequency components and updates the low-frequency component through a global Fourier operator. A local nonlinear branch then processes the high-frequency component together with the updated low-frequency features. This conditioning acts on the features of the current input within each layer: the global spectral update directly informs the local detail correction. It differs from transferring weights between frequency experts or iteratively refining an output prediction. A lead-time-dependent fusion mechanism combines the two branches, while feature-wise affine modulation conditions the layer on the prediction interval. By processing high-frequency information through a shared local branch, FDSR also avoids allocating separate spectral weights to those modes. The prediction interval introduces a complementary consideration. Longer intervals reduce the number of recursive transitions but can make the finite-time mapping harder to approximate; shorter intervals simplify each prediction while requiring more frequent propagation of predicted states Luchtenburg et al. (2014) . We use segmented training and execution to examine this trade-off with F 3 NO. The operator is trained to predict over bounded temporal intervals, and long trajectories are generated by propagating predicted states across segment boundaries. Within each segment, intermediate states are predicted directly from the segment’s initial state and can be evaluated in parallel. FDSR thus determines how spatial information is processed, while segmentation determines the temporal interval over which that processing is learned and applied. We evaluate F 3 NO on the 1D Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation (KSE) Kuramoto (1978) ; Ashinsky (1988) , 1D Burgers’ equation (BE) Burgers (1948) , 2D Navier–Stokes equation (NSE) Temam (2001) , 2D shallow-water equation (SWE) Takamoto et al. (2022) , and 3D Rayleigh–Taylor Instability (RTI) Ohana et al. (2024) . Our experiments assess forecasting accuracy, parameter efficiency, and the effects of spatial resolution and prediction interval. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We develop FDSR, an operator-layer architecture in which updated low-frequency features directly condition nonlinear refinement of high-frequency information, with lead-time-dependent fusion of the spectral and local branches. • We investigate segmented training and execution for finite-time neural operators, examining the trade-off between prediction interval and recursive propagation while enabling parallel prediction within each segment. • We evaluate the framework across five PDE benchmarks and use architectural and execution-mode ablations to characterize when frequency refinement and segmentation improve prediction accuracy and efficiency. 2 Technical Background 2.1 Neural Operators NOs have emerged as a powerful data-driven paradigm for approximating function-to-function mappings, offering a resolution-invariant alternative to traditional numerical solvers Kovachki et al. (2023) . Formally, let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and 𝒰 \mathcal{U} be separable Banach spaces of functions defined on a bounded domain D ⊂ ℝ d D\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} . We seek to learn a non-linear operator G † : 𝒜 → 𝒰 G^{\dagger}:\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{U} that maps an input function a ∈ 𝒜 a\in\mathcal{A} to an output solution u ∈ 𝒰 u\in\mathcal{U} . Next, we conduct a varying-spatial-resolution experiment to evaluate the robustness of the proposed method under changes in the fidelity of the spatial representation. Increasing the spatial resolution introduces higher-frequency modes (i.e., spatial details), which makes learning a flow-map more challenging: the operator must accurately capture interactions across a broader spectral range while maintaining temporal stability. Furthermore, higher resolution typically benefits rollouts by reducing discretization error at each step. By fixing ν = 0.075 \nu=0.075 and varying the resolution in { 32 , 64 , 128 } \{32,64,128\} , this experiment isolates the effect of spatial complexity on different temporal modeling strategies. As shown in Table 2 , prediction error decreases for all methods as spatial resolution increases, reflecting improved representation of local dynamics. Despite the increased spectral complexity at higher resolutions, the proposed segmented flow-map consistently achieves the lowest error across all settings, resulting in 9%–42% improvements compared to the second best performing models. While rollout-based models narrow the performance gap as resolution increases, they remain less accurate than the proposed method even at the highest resolution. This suggests that the advantage of the proposed approach does not arise solely from coarse-grid effects, but from its ability to model finite-time evolution in a manner that remains robust as spatial complexity increases.
